clue.text: Brotherhood from pseudo-historical "tushery" for young folks

definitions.text: Brotherhood from pseudo-historical "tushery" for young folks

parts.words: Brotherhood from pseudo-historical "tushery" for young folks
parts.note: Stevenson dismissed his own Wars of the Roses adventure for boys as 'tushery'; the outlaw fellowship in it gives the book its title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tushery' was Stevenson's word for mock-archaic romance; he used it of his own boys' adventure set in the Wars of the Roses.
explanation.definitionFit: The outlaw fellowship in Stevenson's novel is named after its emblem and gives the book its title.

clue.text: Means of vessel's progress observed" by James

explanation.walkthrough: A ship's propeller is often called its screw. 'observed' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotation of a ship's propeller drives it forward; it is also the title of Henry James's ghost novella.

clue.text: Legendary Longfellow heroine

parts.note: Longfellow's poem The Golden Legend has a peasant girl ready to give her life for Prince Henry; 'Legendary' points at the title

explanation.definitionFit: The self-sacrificing maiden of Longfellow's The Golden Legend bears this name.

clue.text: New "milords" all, followers of this doctrine

indicators.note: New says the letters of the next two words are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Every lord, newly titled, signs up to some creed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges MILORDS and ALL. The Lollards were followers of Wycliffe, so the answer is the doctrine they followed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lollards' creed was the reforming teaching of John Wycliffe, a body of religious belief.

clue.text: Row stirred up by Steinbeck

parts.note: row looks like a quarrel but is the street in Monterey that names Steinbeck's novel; the missing first word of that title is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novel is set on a Monterey street of fish-packing plants, Cannery Row.

clue.text: Some paper customarily refuted in France — showing insights

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A newspaper habitually quotes rebuttals from French sources.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing for quick glimpses or flashes of understanding, sharp observations.

clue.text: Divide and thus hold sway. Mark her words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divide and rule' is the proverb; to rule a page is to mark lines on it to write on.
explanation.definitionFit: Divide and conquer, the maxim of governing; and to draw straight lines on paper for writing on.

clue.text: Humorist to provide poem in western home

indicators.note: in places the poem inside the western home

parts.note: a house is a home
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A comic writer is asked to supply verse for a house out west.
explanation.definitionFit: P. G. Wodehouse, creator of Jeeves and Wooster, is the best-known English comic novelist.

clue.text: Thomas's revealed a past brittle with relics

definitions.text: Thomas's revealed a past brittle with relics

parts.words: Thomas's revealed a past brittle with relics
parts.note: the quoted phrase comes from a poem by R. S. Thomas about the country of his birth, whose title is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas is R. S. Thomas, the Welsh poet-priest, not Dylan.
explanation.definitionFit: R. S. Thomas's poem describing his nation's scenery speaks of 'a past brittle with relics'.

clue.text: Nero's lady reincarnated in Elizabethan play

indicators.note: reincarnated says the letters of the emperor's lady come back to life in a new form

parts.note: taken as written, the S included

explanation.surface: An emperor's consort is reborn in a sixteenth-century drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reincarnated' rearranges NEROS and LADY. Thomas Lodge's Elizabethan romance was the source of As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Lodge's Elizabethan pastoral romance, Shakespeare's source for As You Like It.

clue.text: Put up 2's creator

explanation.walkthrough: The '2' must be read as 9: Thomas Lodge wrote Rosalynde, the answer at 9-across, not the Longfellow heroine at 2.
explanation.definitionFit: To house someone as a guest; Thomas Lodge was the author of Rosalynde.

clue.text: Final letter from Homer?

parts.note: looks like a poet's last epistle, but means the last character of the alphabet Homer wrote in, Greek

explanation.definitionFit: The last character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: How artist can make a strong impression

definitions.text: How artist can make a strong impression

parts.words: How artist can make a strong impression
parts.note: a strong impression sounds like a lasting effect, but here it is a print taken from a plate bitten by acid

explanation.definitionFit: Printmakers incise a design into a metal plate with acid to print from it.

clue.text: She starts Rochester's history, yet stops

indicators.note: starts says the opening letters of the following four words are taken

explanation.surface: A woman begins telling the tale of Mr Rochester, then breaks off.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Rhys wrote Wide Sargasso Sea, the history of Rochester's first wife before Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Rhys, the woman novelist who gave Rochester's first wife a back story.

clue.text: Novelist shows leaders take a relaxed position over model painting

parts.note: the van is the leading part of an army, those in front
to sit is to take a rested posture
the Model T Ford gives T
painting is a form of art

explanation.surface: An author is seen as front-runners lounging over a picture of a model.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Vansittart was a prolific English historical novelist. 'over' just places the pieces in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Vansittart was a twentieth-century English writer of historical fiction.

clue.text: "There are days when spelling — simply doesn't count" (A. A. Milne)

definitions.text: "There are days when spelling — simply doesn't count" (A. A. Milne)

parts.words: "There are days when spelling — simply doesn't count" (A. A. Milne)
parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh's remark about his wobbly spelling; the missing word is a day of the week

explanation.definitionFit: Pooh says some days spelling one particular weekday is not important; the gap is that weekday.

clue.text: Passé epic? reworked and presented by Eliot

indicators.note: reworked says the letters of the outdated epic are reshaped into a new form

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned epic gets a makeover from George Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reworked' rearranges PASSE and EPIC. Eppie Cass is the girl raised by Silas Marner.
explanation.definitionFit: The foundling adopted by Silas Marner in George Eliot's novel, born to Godfrey Cass.

clue.text: Chekhov's Nina said that a man came along, saw it and killed it, just to pass the time

definitions.text: Chekhov's Nina said that a man came along, saw it and killed it, just to pass the time

parts.words: Chekhov's Nina said that a man came along, saw it and killed it, just to pass the time
parts.note: Nina in Chekhov's play likens herself to a shore bird shot idly by a passing man; the bird is also the title

explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's play takes its name from the shot bird Nina compares herself to.

clue.text: In view, like Elizabeth George's evidence

explanation.definitionFit: Laid open to sight; Elizabeth George's book of stories is The Evidence Exposed.

clue.text: Epitome of renaissance man

parts.note: the polymath painter and engineer of fifteenth-century Italy is the classic model of the many-talented person

explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo, painter, inventor and anatomist, is the standard example of the universal genius.

clue.text: "A copper — for the table, which is very pretty, and they demand £6 or £7 for one" (S. Pepys)

definitions.text: "A copper — for the table, which is very pretty, and they demand £6 or £7 for one" (S. Pepys)

parts.words: "A copper — for the table, which is very pretty, and they demand £6 or £7 for one" (S. Pepys)
parts.note: Pepys's diary admires a copper vessel for holding water at table; the missing word names that container

explanation.definitionFit: A tank for water; Pepys priced a decorative copper one for the dining table.

clue.text: Cleopatra said that none but Antony should — Antony

definitions.text: Cleopatra said that none but Antony should — Antony

parts.words: Cleopatra said that none but Antony should — Antony
parts.note: Shakespeare's queen says no one but Antony himself should defeat Antony; the missing verb is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: To defeat; in Shakespeare's play only Antony may overcome Antony.

clue.text: Durrell protagonist in debacle at Cairo

indicators.note: in says the name sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A character from Durrell is caught up in an Egyptian fiasco.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter who names the last book of Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet.

clue.text: S. M. Eisenstein classic, with terrible omission

parts.words: S. M. Eisenstein classic, with terrible omission
parts.note: Eisenstein's film of the Russian tsar, with the words 'the Terrible' dropped from its title

explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the tsar in Eisenstein's two-part film, without his epithet.

clue.text: Bundle offering zero tolerance approach to punctuation

definitions.text: offering zero tolerance approach to punctuation

explanation.definitionFit: A tied bale of hay; and Lynne Truss, whose book on grammar is subtitled The Zero Tolerance Approach to Punctuation.

clue.text: Poe's Roderick involved, we might suppose, with the worst of jerry-builders

definitions.text: Poe's Roderick involved, we might suppose, with the worst of jerry-builders

parts.words: Poe's Roderick involved, we might suppose, with the worst of jerry-builders
parts.note: Roderick's family seat in Poe's tale cracks and collapses into the tarn, as if shoddily built

explanation.definitionFit: Roderick's surname in Poe's tale of the falling house.

clue.text: Valley of romantic novelist

explanation.definitionFit: A small wooded hollow; Ethel M. Dell wrote popular romances.

clue.text: Avoid some part of "Little Eva, dead at last"

indicators.note: some part of says the answer lies within the quoted phrase

explanation.surface: A request to dodge a passage about the death of a little girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Eva is the child whose death is mourned in Uncle Tom's Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodge or escape something.

clue.text: Salamis as offered at Roman circus?

definitions.text: Salamis as offered at Roman circus?

parts.words: Salamis as offered at Roman circus?
parts.note: Salamis was a famous sea battle; Romans flooded arenas to stage mock fights between ships

explanation.definitionFit: A staged sea fight put on as public spectacle in ancient Rome.

clue.text: Kipling's musketeers?

parts.note: like Dumas's trio, Kipling's book follows three comrades, private soldiers in India

explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's stories about Mulvaney, Ortheris and Learoyd, a trio of privates.
